title: Tetley acquisition — the first great Indian cross-border purchase
statement: Ratan Tata bought the 170-year-old British tea brand Tetley for roughly £271 million — larger than Tata Tea itself at the time — reversing the colonial-era relationship between Indian producer and British brand.
outcome: Tetley became the platform for Tata Global Beverages and proved the post-liberalization Indian multinational could integrate an iconic Western consumer brand; Ratan Tata later cited it as the deal that taught the group it could buy abroad.

title: Corus Steel acquisition
statement: Tata Steel paid $12 billion for the Anglo-Dutch steelmaker Corus, an acquisition nearly ten times its own size, to gain European footprint and move up the value chain.
outcome: The timing near the commodity peak burdened Tata Steel with debt through the subsequent decade and remains the group's most criticized deal — Ratan Tata defended it as a strategic necessity whose cycle timing, not logic, failed.

title: Jaguar Land Rover acquisition from Ford
statement: At the depth of the 2008 crisis, Tata Motors bought Jaguar Land Rover from Ford for $2.3 billion, roughly a third of what Ford had paid for the marques.
outcome: JLR became the profit engine of Tata Motors, powering its transformation into a global automaker; the purchase is ranked among the greatest turnaround acquisitions of the era.

title: The Tata Nano — engineering the one-lakh car
statement: Ratan Tata personally championed a rear-engined, sub-$2,000 family car meant to move Indian families off two-wheelers safely — one of the most audacious cost-engineering projects in automotive history.
outcome: The Nano's product brilliance never overcame its marketing as a 'poor man's car' and the Singur factory controversy; production ended by 2018. Tata treated it as an engineering triumph and a commercial lesson.

title: Mistry dismissal and the battle for the group's soul
statement: Ratan Tata moved to remove Cyrus Mistry as chairman of Tata Sons, restoring the trust-ownership principle against a successor he judged had strayed from the group's philanthropic and governance traditions.
outcome: The boardroom war ran through Indian courts and the NCLT for years; ultimately the Tata Trusts' control structure held, and Ratan Tata returned as interim chairman before N. Chandrasekaran's appointment.
